headline: Black Friday Shoppers Spend Big on Tech Despite Tight Budgets

paragraphs.text: Americans spent heavily on consumer electronics and software on Black Friday, one of the biggest shopping days of the holiday season, as they looked for deals on laptops, televisions and video games.

Black Friday spending in the United States rose 5.8 percent this year compared with last year, with gains both in stores and online, according to data from Mastercard SpendingPulse, which measures sales from all payment types. Its figures are not adjusted for inflation and exclude purchases of gasoline and autos.

The numbers were generally in line with forecasts. Americans had been expected to open their wallets this holiday season, even as their household budgets have been strained by higher costs for gas and groceries brought on by the war in Iran.

Electronics and software had a strong month overall, bolstered by the release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19. Black Friday sales in the category rose 7.9 percent this year, according to Mastercard. Apparel had a slower month, but picked up on Black Friday, with a 4.4 percent jump in sales. Jewelry sales rose 4.6 percent.

“It’s a robust output,” said Michelle Meyer, the chief economist of the Mastercard Economics Institute. “At the moment, it definitely looks like consumers are indeed out there shopping and prioritizing what matters most to them.”
More details on what consumers are buying are set to be released in the coming weeks as the holiday shopping rush unfolds.
In September, Mastercard said it expected total retail sales to grow 5.5 percent this year in the period from Nov. 1 through Christmas Eve.
But the financial pressures have made shoppers more discerning. They have given priority to value and been comparing prices, while using sales events as an opportunity to stock up on essential items.
Retailers, in turn, have rolled out low-price gift sections and cut prices on thousands of items to lure consumers worried about money.

Several of America’s biggest retailers, including Walmart, Target and TJX, which owns TJ Maxx and Marshalls, raised their financial outlooks ahead of Black Friday. John Furner, the chief executive of Walmart, told investors this month that he expected a “pretty strong” season.
“The words we would use to describe the customer are stable, resilient,” Mr. Furner said.

Best Buy, the largest specialty consumer electronics retailer in the United States, also raised its guidance this past week and said its computer and gaming categories had performed better than expected in its most recent quarter.

“Our core customers continue to demonstrate remarkable resiliency and engagement,” Jason Bonfig, the new chief executive of Best Buy, told investors. “And we are also seeing growth in new and re-engaged customers.”

Black Friday is no longer the spectacle that it once was, with long lines for big-screen televisions and door-busting deals. Instead, shoppers are turning increasingly to online purchases and retailers are spreading sales over months. Still, retailers nodded to those past promotions with deep discounts for TVs, laptops and smart home products, like $350 off a 48-inch Samsung TV on Amazon.

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.8 billion in retail sales globally in its first day, according to Rockstar Games, the developer, in what it called “the biggest entertainment launch in history.” Video game sales can have a halo effect on related hardware and accessories, such as game consoles and headphones.
Ms. Meyer, the Mastercard economist, said she expected the momentum for tech sales to persist through the holiday season, as shoppers buy for themselves and gifts for friends and family.
Retailers typically see a lull in sales in early December after Cyber Monday, until the run-up to Christmas Day as Americans scramble to finish their gift lists.
“If we continue to get into the end of the year with strong job creation, a low unemployment rate and steady wage growth, I think the consumers will be equipped to to spend,” Ms. Meyer said.
